2. What the energy-distance inequality now gives

Let

 $A=H_{\mathrm{code}},\qquad
A\succeq \frac{\sigma}{N}D_{\mathcal C},$ and let  $P_r$  project onto the span of all weight-at-most- $r$  Pauli errors applied to the codespace.

By the definition of the distance operator,

 $D_{\mathcal C}\succeq(r+1)(I-P_r).$ Hence, for every state  $\rho$ ,

 $\boxed{
\operatorname{Tr}((I-P_r)\rho)
\le
\frac{N\,\operatorname{Tr}(A\rho)}{\sigma(r+1)}.
}                                                   \tag{2}$ This remains valid with an arbitrary reference system.

When  $p=\operatorname{Tr}(P_r\rho)>0$ , define

 $\rho_r=\frac{P_r\rho P_r}{p}.$ Projection of a purification, followed by tracing out the purifying system, gives

 $\boxed{
\frac12\|\rho-\rho_r\|_1
\le
\sqrt{\frac{N\,\operatorname{Tr}(A\rho)}
{\sigma(r+1)}}.
}                                                   \tag{3}$ For  $r=\lfloor\rho_*N\rfloor$ , equations (2)–(3) provide a genuine constant-scale conversion from small code energy to proximity to the coherent correctable subspace.

That is stronger than a count of nonzero violated checks. It nevertheless certifies protected storage, not an executed computation. Logical transformations within the codespace have zero code energy. Code energy alone therefore cannot enforce prescribed initialization, propagation, or rejection.
